summary.short: Qatar's Law No. 13 of 2016 governs personal data processed electronically. It requires controllers to obtain consent, give notice, limit use, secure data and restrict cross-border transfers, with stricter rules for sensitive data and children's websites. It sets fines and gave existing processing six months to conform.
summary.long: The law applies to personal data processed electronically or collected for electronic processing, and excludes purely personal or family use and processing for official statistics (Art. 2). Individuals may withdraw consent, object, request deletion and correction (Art. 5), and receive access, notice and a copy of their data for a fee not exceeding the service cost (Art. 6). Controllers must obtain consent unless processing serves a legitimate purpose (Art. 4), give prior notice of purposes and processing (Art. 9), keep data relevant and no longer than necessary (Art. 10), and adopt internal measures including data protection officers, training, complaint systems and audits (Art. 11). Controllers and processors must protect personal data (Art. 13), and controllers must notify the competent administration and individuals of serious breaches (Art. 14). Controllers may not take decisions that restrict cross-border data flows, except where processing violates the law or would cause serious harm (Art. 15). Sensitive data, including racial origin, children, health, religion, marital status and criminal offences, may be processed only with a permit from the competent administration (Art. 16). Operators of websites directed at children must give notice, obtain parental consent and meet further conditions (Art. 17). Exemptions apply for national security, public interest and certain legal duties (Arts. 18 to 21). Direct marketing by electronic communication requires prior consent and an opt-out (Art. 22). Violations are punishable by fines (Arts. 23 to 25). Individuals may complain, and the competent administration may order a remedy, with appeal to the Minister (Art. 26). Contracts made in breach of the law are void (Art. 28). Existing data handlers had six months from the effective date to conform (Art. 30).},

notes: Relations are taken from the preamble citations and from Art. 2. The preamble recitals do not state which powers each cited instrument confers, so they are coded as legal_basis without further specification. The Official Statistics Law row combines the Art. 2 exclusion with the preamble citation; the preamble also records that it was amended by Law No. (4) of 2015, which is not an amendment made by this law. Art. 26 reads 'خلال مدة . تحددها' with the period missing from the text as provided, so the compliance period cannot be taken from it. Art. 30 gives six months from 'تاريخ العمل به' without stating the entry-into-force date in the text. Only Art. 2 and Art. 30 interact with an external instrument or date; no amendment or repeal clause appears in the text. Quotes are from the document as provided, which shows OCR-style spacing artefacts.

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff in the text changes legal treatment. Fine amounts in Arts. 23-25 are enforcement (penalty maxima), and the six-month compliance period in Art. 30 and the 60-day appeal periods in Art. 26 are procedural time limits (events). Art. 16 lets the Minister add special-nature data categories and Art. 17 applies to children without a numeric age, so neither yields a threshold row. Art. 6(3) refers to a fee not exceeding the service cost, which is not a number.
